blocks.cap: The Hozumi fox shrine in upper Kita

blocks.p: The old man was sweeping when Rei arrived, and that was the first wrong thing. The stones were already clean. He swept them anyway, with the slow going-nowhere stroke of a man keeping his hands busy so they would not shake.

blocks.cap: Miyamoto Kazuo, head priest of the Hozumi shrine

blocks.p: Miyamoto Kazuo was sixty-six, the head priest, a kannushi in white and indigo with his white hair tied in a small topknot. He told Rei who he was before Rei could ask. His father had kept this shrine before him, and his grandfather before that. His line had warded this ground for two hundred years. Every Obon a hand in his family renewed the wards that ringed the precinct. He recited it the way a man recites the deed to a house he is afraid is no longer his.

The shrine itself was almost nothing. Two stone foxes with lichen grown into their grins. A vermilion gate gone the colour of dried blood. An old camphor tree that Miyamoto bowed to as he passed it, out of a habit older than thought. Under a little roof stood a stone basin of still water, where visitors rinsed their hands before they troubled the god. A three-coloured cat sat on the rim of the basin and stared into it without drinking. It was the kind of place the city forgets so thoroughly that the forgetting becomes a kind of protection.

Miyamoto would not let Rei near the basin until he had said what he had called him to say. He said it badly, in pieces, looking at the broom. For two hundred years the water in that basin had held the lanterns. Every Obon the neighbourhood strung paper lights along the lane, and every Obon the basin caught them and held them doubled and trembling on its skin. That doubling, Miyamoto said, was how a keeper knew the boundary was holding. A shrine that reflects is a shrine that is still listening.
"This week the lanterns are lit," he said. "The lane is strung. And the water lies there flat and black and holds nothing. No lights. No roof beam. When you lean over it, your own face is not there."

Both of Rei's registers came up at that, slow and certain, the low one and the searching one, and for once they did not disagree. He had spent the week learning the particular wrongness of a thing that had stopped answering. Gin's flat. The address in no file. The cases closed too clean. He recognised the same shape in an old man's basin.

Miyamoto set the broom against the gate and took a packet of cigarettes from his sleeve. His hands shook too much for the match. Rei took out his lighter without thinking and held the flame for him. The old man drew on it, nodded his thanks, and seemed to steady.

"I am too old to read what has gone wrong," he said, "and too frightened to leave it unread. I sent word to the Division. The Division sent a form. I sent word to the temple. The temple sent prayers." He looked at Rei properly for the first time. "You are the only one who came up the steps instead of mailing something down them."
Rei asked him what the wards actually were. He knew how the CVD did it, with glyphs and grades and paperwork. This was not that.

"We do not fight what comes," Miyamoto said. "My father used to say Shinto does not exorcise so much as it tidies. Every night I walk the grounds. The lamps, the salt at the gate at dusk, the gate itself. I keep the place clean and named and in good repair, and things that should not cross find it does not want them. Once a year, at Obon, the cords are re-tied, and the water is asked to keep watching. That is all. It has been enough for two hundred years." He blew smoke at the camphor tree, then apologised to it. "It has been enough until this week."

Up close the water was worse than Miyamoto had described. He had described an absence, and an absence is at least a clean thing. This was not clean. The basin was full to the lip and dead still. No wind reached it under the roof. When Rei leaned over it, the lanterns behind him did not appear, and neither did he. But the surface was not blank. It was busy, the way a held breath is busy. Under the flatness there was a faint slow churn, like something turning over far down in water that was only a hand deep.
The cat stepped down from the rim and moved away from him, its tail low.

Rei put two fingers on the stone rim, not on the water, and let the read come. It came wrong. A shrine basin should taste of two hundred Obons of cupped hands and rinsed mouths and small honest fears asked into the dark. This one tasted of all that. Then, underneath, it tasted of a single clean cut. Something woven had been unwoven, neatly, by someone who knew exactly which thread to lift.

He crouched and looked longer than was wise. The longer he looked, the more certain both registers became. The water was not failing to reflect him. It was choosing not to, the way a person who has been told something unkind about a stranger declines to meet his eye. Somewhere in the basin's long history a boundary had been strung between the lane and whatever the lane was built to forget. Reflection kept it taut. Every day the water proved that the world on this side was solid enough to throw an image back. Pull the proof and the boundary goes slack.

The lanterns burned three steps behind him, gold and doubled along the lane. At the rim of this stone they stopped dead, as though the basin had been excused from the evening. It had been set apart, quietly, so that something could use it without the neighbourhood noticing the seam.

When he took his fingers off the rim, the churn under the surface settled the way water settles after a fish has turned. For one held instant before it went flat, the black skin showed him a face after all. It was not his. It was a calm, pleasant, entirely reasonable face that he had been learning the shape of all week without yet being allowed to name it. Then the water lay still and gave nothing.
"Did you see anything?" Miyamoto asked, in the small voice of a man who already knew.

The honest answer was that Rei had seen the Healer's bedside manner wearing a two-hundred-year-old shrine like a clean white coat. He said, "Yes." The lane kept burning. The basin kept its peace, which was the wrong kind of peace. It had been arranged.

The shrine office was one mat wide, behind the gate. A curl of cedar smoke rose from a dish in the corner, as it had in this room, Miyamoto said, for as long as anyone remembered. The ledger of renewals was older than the bulb and older than the table. It was a stack of bound books in a cloth-wrapped pile, each one a generation of Obons recorded in the cramped hand of whoever held the broom that century.

Miyamoto turned to this year's page with the reluctance of a man opening a wound to show the doctor where it hurts. The entry was there in an unfamiliar hand. It was not his and not his line's. It was a clean modern script, and in the place where the keeper records who renewed the wards it had written a single phrase. A friend assisted.

"He came in the spring," Miyamoto said, looking at the stranger's writing in his family's book. "A soft-spoken man. A healer, he said. He had heard the old keeper's hands were failing." He held up his own hands and let Rei see the tremor. "I have no one yet to pass the duty to. He knew that too. He offered, for nothing, for the simple rightness of it, to help me renew the work I could no longer manage alone." His voice did the thing voices do when kindness turns out to have been the knife. "He was so very kind. He asked only that I let him tie the last knot himself. The last knot, he said, is the one that matters."

Rei read the entry and both registers went cold and quiet. He had seen this hand before, or its work. The same neat economy. The same gift offered into exactly the gap a person is most ashamed of. It was in Gin's ledger of favours. It was in every place this week where Yushiro the Healer had reached in through someone's worst small fear and adjusted one thread while they wept with gratitude.

The wards had not been breached. They had been re-tied, expertly, by a guest invited in through the front gate by the keeper's own grief at his failing hands. And the last knot, the one that held the reflection, the one that kept the boundary listening, had been tied to give way on a schedule. This week. Obon, when the membrane over all of Kita was thinnest and every shrine in the district was straining to hold its own small piece of the wall. Pull one keeper's stone loose now and there is no flood. There is a draught. A single clean current through one forgotten shed of a shrine, feeding the larger thinning Yushiro had been working toward all along.

Miyamoto wanted to know what Rei would do. Under that, he wanted to know what he himself had done. Had his failing hands made this, or would it have come anyway? There was no answer Rei could give that would return the spring to him, the morning he had been so grateful to be helped.

Rei went back out and stood at the basin with his hands in his pockets. The temptation came quietly, and it came in a reasonable voice. The Healer did not know he had found this. Leave the knot as it was, and the shrine would go on failing on its schedule, and the small cold current through the water would show him exactly where the larger thinning ran and what it was for. He could sit on these steps every night until Obon ended and take notes. It would cost an old man his basin, and a boundary his family had kept for two hundred years, and whatever else came through a draught while Rei stood beside it with a pencil.

blocks.cap: The three-coloured cat of the shrine

blocks.p: The cat came and sat beside his foot and looked up at him. Rei thought about Gin, who would have closed it without a second thought. Gin sat up all night with widows and wrote the case files afterwards. The voice that wanted the window open sounded sensible, and that was exactly what frightened him about it. It was the Healer's arithmetic. A hole in a neighbourhood's wall, kept open because the hole was useful. He would not learn to think like that.
"We close it," he said. "But first I need to read where it goes."

Miyamoto did not argue. He fetched the cords from the office, hemp twisted with paper, and showed Rei the knots his father had taught him. Rei went back to the basin and put his whole hand flat on the stone this time. He let the current run through him for as long as he could stand it. It was cold and steady and it ran one way. North. Toward the river, and past it, toward the old ground beyond the freight line where the city's maps went vague. He held that direction in his mind like a compass bearing and then he took his hand away.

The re-tying took the rest of the afternoon. Miyamoto's hands knew every knot and could not hold them steady. Rei's hands were steady and knew nothing. So Rei held the cords taut and the old man tied. When they reached the last knot, Rei read along the cord with his fingertips and found the place where the stranger's thread had been lifted, the single strand pulled loose and laid back so that it would slip. He showed Miyamoto. Miyamoto bowed to the camphor tree, then to the basin, then bent and tied it the way his father had tied it. It was a plain knot. It did not slip.

The evening came as it always did on the third night. The neighbourhood came out. Old women in cotton yukata. Children with fox masks pushed up on their foreheads. They filed past the little shrine, clapped twice and bowed, and none of them felt the seam Rei had spent the day standing inside. That was the mercy and the horror of a forgotten shrine. Its failing was invisible to exactly the people it failed.

Then Miyamoto lit the last lantern at the gate, and the basin caught it. The light came back doubled and trembling on the water's skin, and then the next one, and the next, until the whole gold string of the lane was held under the little roof the way it had been held for two hundred summers. The three-coloured cat jumped up onto the rim, looked into the water, and drank.

Miyamoto found Rei at the gate and read his face the way old keepers read water. What passed between them was not exactly gratitude. Rei had not given him back the spring. Both of them knew the kind stranger would come again, to some other failing pair of hands, with the same soft offer and the same patient knot. But the old man took Rei's hand in both of his, dry and light as paper.

"My father used to say the shrine does not protect the neighbourhood from the thing on the other side," he said. "It protects the thing on the other side from the neighbourhood's forgetting. It keeps it small and named and bounded. A forgotten thing grows. A watched thing waits."

Rei had restored the watching. Somewhere across the thinning city, the Healer had lost one quiet draught. It was still one stone further along a wall it meant to bring down by Obon's end. But Rei had something now that he had not had that morning. He knew which way the draught had been running.

He walked home the long way, past the small Inari shrine a hundred metres north of Gin's building. He had passed it a thousand times without looking. Tonight he stopped. Gin had written about this shrine in the district pages of the archive, and Rei remembered the note now.

lines: Jujo Shrine. Small Inari shrine, 100m north of the archive building.
Continuous traditional maintenance has produced genuine veil-structure function... a stabilized point, not a thin spot.
Entity activity in 150m radius is measurably lower. I used this for documentation work requiring minimal ambient disruption.

blocks.p: So that was part of why Gin did his writing at home. He had been sitting inside the shrine's quiet.

An old woman was refilling the lamp at the fox statues. She was small and straight-backed, in a grey work apron, and she watched Rei come under the gate without any warmth at all. He did not speak first. He rinsed his hands at the basin, bowed twice, clapped twice, bowed once more, the way he had been taught as a boy. Only then did he turn to her.

Her name was Ishikawa Tsuneko. She was seventy-one. She had kept Jūjō Inari for thirty-one years, and her grandmother had kept it before her, and her family had done the work here since the Meiji era. She did not call it ward work or symbol work. She called it the duties. Which nights needed the salt, which corners needed the lamp, which visitors were carrying something they should not have brought up the steps. She did not think of herself as a practitioner of anything. She only knew the shrine worked.
Rei looked into her basin. The lanterns from the street were there, small and doubled and steady.
"Has anyone offered to help you with the duties?" he asked. "This year. Someone kind."

She gave him a long, evaluating look. "The government has asked to help me three times," she said. "I said no. The other ones, the ones without an office, have asked twice. I said no to them too." She put her hand on the basin's rim, and when she lifted it, Rei felt the stone was warmer than the evening, as if she had left something of herself in it. "I do not let anyone else do the duties. A thing you hand to a stranger is not your duty any more."

Gin's archive said the people without an office had decided to leave her alone, because her work was the reason this corner of Jūjō had stayed steady for decades, and interfering with her would break something they relied on. Rei suspected she knew that. He suspected she would never say so.

He thanked her and went down the steps as the drums started somewhere toward the river. It was the slow Obon rhythm that calls the dead home for their three nights and then sends them off again. The sound found the loose thing in him that had been pulled tight all day. Down at the embankment the first paper boats were going onto the black water, holding their small lights out for the dead. The dead were very close this week. They were getting closer by exactly as many stones as the Healer could talk a grieving keeper into loosening. Tonight there was one stone fewer. And two old people in Kita who would not hand their duty to anyone.
